blocks.text: …open the box under the dashboard. He made me promise I'd wait until you found the receiver. My name is Lacey. I'm your sister."

I sat in that truck for a long time with my hands on the steering wheel. Then I reached under the dashboard and found a small steel box held in place with two magnets. Inside was a safe-deposit key, an envelope with my name on it in my father's handwriting, and a second photograph: the same little girl from the prison picture, a few years older, sitting on the tailgate of this truck.

Lacey was transmitting from a cheap two-way radio rig in her car, parked on a gravel road a quarter mile from my father's barn. Dad had built the receiver himself years ago. He was a mechanic who could make anything talk to anything.
She was terrified, she explained when I drove out to meet her, because a man in a silver truck had been following her for three days.

In 1979, when I was five, my father spent most of a year working at a garage in Shreveport, Louisiana, driving home to us on weekends. While he was there, he had an affair with a woman named Darlene. Late one night, the garage owner set fire to his own building for the insurance money. Nobody was hurt, but the owner needed someone to blame. He chose Darlene, who did the books and had a key. My father had seen the owner with the gas cans. But the owner had friends in the sheriff's office and threatened my father's life if he testified. My father ran home to Arkansas.
Darlene was convicted of arson and insurance fraud and served eleven years.

She gave birth to Lacey in prison. My father, sick with guilt, took Lacey on weekends when she was little, driving to the prison to visit her mother. That's the photo. He told my mother he was hauling parts.

Years later, the garage owner, dying, wrote my father a letter confessing everything and asking forgiveness. Dad kept it in a safe-deposit box with a sworn statement of his own. He was too ashamed to use it while he was alive. He left it to me.
"You're the only person who can open that box," Lacey said. "And Mama's eighty-one. She doesn't have a lot of time left to have her name cleared."
The man in the silver truck was the garage owner's son, who had heard about my father's death and was afraid of what might be in the will.
He was arrested two days later outside Lacey's motel for stalking and carrying an unregistered gun.

We opened the safe-deposit box together. With the confession and my father's statement, a Louisiana innocence project petitioned the court. Darlene's conviction was vacated eight months later. She was in a wheelchair in the front row, holding Lacey's hand and mine.
I'm restoring the truck now. Lacey helps on weekends. She knows more about engines than I do. Dad taught her too.
We left the receiver in. Sometimes, when she's driving home, she turns on her radio and says goodnight.
